passage:
Tuesday. Swati shoved her phone across the desk. "Read this." A report said the preacher told followers to give up luxuries, while he lived in a big house and took money from their donations. Neelam read it twice and felt heat in the face. "I sent him my pocket money."
Thursday. Neelam deleted every saved video, jaw tight. "I feel so stupid. And so angry." Swati said, "You were hoping. That's not stupid."
Sunday. Neelam sat on the terrace, thinking of one talk about being patient with others. It had helped her with her little brother. She kept that note and thought, that part was true anyway.

qa.q: What did Neelam find out about how the preacher lived?
qa.a: Neelam found that the preacher told followers to give up luxuries while living in a big house and taking money from their donations.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling on Thursday, and why?
qa.a: Neelam felt stupid and angry, since Neelam had sent the preacher pocket money and now saw the gap between his words and his life.

qa.q: What could Neelam keep from the teachings?
qa.a: The parts that proved true in life, such as patience with others, which helped with Neelam's little brother, while dropping the rest.

qa.q: How does Swati see Neelam's hope?
qa.a: Swati does not think it was stupid; she says "You were hoping", so hope itself was not the mistake.

grounding: Neelam discovers the preacher lives against his own words and earns from followers, feels foolish and angry, and keeps the teachings that were true.

passage:
For a year, Thabo had watched every video by the pastor from Pretoria who preached simple living. "Wealth is a trap," he said, in a plain white shirt. Thabo gave away his old sneakers to a younger boy because of him.

Then, in the school library in Johannesburg, his friend Emil pushed his phone across the table. An article. Photos of the pastor's three luxury cars, his mansion, and a new "Prosperity Pack" his followers could buy.

Thabo stared. His face went hot. "I defended him. At my uncle's braai. I told everyone he was different."

"You weren't stupid," Emil said. "He was good at it."

Thabo walked home angry, at the pastor and at himself. That night he sat on his bed and wrote two lists. What he'd been told that was true: be generous, don't chase things, help younger kids. What was a lie: the man.

He unfollowed the channel. He kept the first list taped inside his cupboard.

qa.q: What did Thabo give away because of the pastor?
qa.a: Thabo gave away his old sneakers to a younger boy.

qa.q: What was Thabo feeling on the walk home?
qa.a: Thabo felt angry at the pastor and at himself, and foolish for having defended him.

qa.q: Why was writing two lists a wise response?
qa.a: It let Thabo keep the true lessons, like generosity, while rejecting the man, so he did not throw away the good or blame himself for hoping.

qa.q: How does Emil see Thabo's mistake?
qa.a: Emil sees it kindly, saying Thabo was not stupid and that the pastor was simply good at fooling people.

grounding: It shows a teen who discovers the preacher he admired lives against his words and earns from followers, feels foolish and angry, and keeps the true teachings without blaming himself.

passage:
In the school computer lab in Kozhikode, Imran sat very still in front of the screen. Manjula ma'am, who ran the lab, noticed he hadn't typed anything for ten minutes.

"Imran?"

He turned the monitor towards her. A news report: the online scholar he had followed for two years, the one who preached humility and poverty, had been found with a luxury flat abroad and a donation scheme that paid him directly.

"I sent him my Eid money last year," Imran said quietly. "I told my cousins he was the only real one. I feel like an idiot."

Manjula ma'am pulled up a chair. "What did you learn from him that was good?"

He thought. "To pray on time. To be honest in business. To be kind to my younger brother."

"Are those still true?"

"…Yes."

"Then keep those. Drop him. And don't punish yourself for hoping someone was good. That hope is a good thing in you."

qa.q: What did Imran send the scholar last year?
qa.a: Imran sent him his Eid money.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling as he looked at the report?
qa.a: Imran felt betrayed and foolish, even calling himself an idiot, after defending the scholar to his cousins.

qa.q: How did Manjula ma'am help Imran sort through what happened?
qa.a: She asked what good he had learned, helped him keep those lessons, and told him not to punish himself for hoping.

qa.q: How might Imran's cousins react if he tells them?
qa.a: They might tease him a little, but they may also feel relieved and respect him for admitting it honestly.

grounding: It shows a teen who discovers the preacher he admired lives against his teachings and profits from followers, feeling foolish and angry, and keeping what was true without blaming himself for hope.
